## Same Levers, Different Regime {.center}

Last lecture: **intermediary liability, takedown regimes, the DSA**, all in democracies.

Today: the **same legal levers** in China, Russia, Iran, and the states that copy them.

- **Licensing** · **intermediary liability** · **real-name registration**
- **Data localization** · **takedown orders** · **shutdown authority**

**Question:** if the EU can order a platform to remove content, what exactly is different
when Russia does it?

::: {.notes}
• Open with the question; take two or three answers before showing anything.<br>• Your claim to test out loud: the difference is rarely the lever itself; it is what the law lets the state call illegal, and whether anyone can say no.<br>• Book: §4.1.1 (to be written from this lecture); §4.1 for the democratic baseline.
:::

## The Authoritarian Legal Toolkit

| Lever | Democratic version (earlier lectures) | Authoritarian version (today) |
|---|---|---|
| **Licensing** | Telecom licences, spectrum | All international traffic through **state gateways**; VPNs need a licence |
| **Intermediary liability** | §230 immunity; DSA notice and action | Operator **must find and delete** prohibited content |
| **Takedown orders** | Court or regulator orders, appealable | Agency orders on a **clock** (Vietnam 24 h; China "immediately") |
| **Real-name registration** | Age assurance (Australia's under-16 ban) | Account tied to **ID or phone number** before posting |
| **Data localization** | GDPR transfer rules | Data **stored at home**, handed over on request |
| **Network control** | No filtering mandate; shutdowns rare (India the exception) | **Mandated filtering boxes**; shutdowns by decree |

::: {.notes}
• Walk the rows quickly; each democratic cell is a callback to the legal lecture.<br>• Ask: which rows would you object to *as written*, before knowing which country passed them?<br>• Hold the comparison for later; this slide only establishes that the toolkit is shared.
:::

## What Makes the Same Law Work Differently?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Vague offences**

- "Fabricating or spreading **false information**"
- "**Extremism**," "**undermining** national unity"
- "**Subversion** of state power"

The state defines the offence **after** the speech.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**No independent recourse**

- Orders come from an **agency**, not a court
- Courts are **not independent** of the executive
- Orders are **secret** or unpublished

The platform has **no one to appeal to**, so it complies **in advance**.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
• This is the frame for the rest of the hour: watch for vagueness and recourse on every country slide.<br>• Tie back to "Law Taxes Speech Without Banning It" from the legal lecture: when the offence is vague, the chilling effect does the work.<br>• Question for you to answer in your own words: is vagueness a bug these laws tolerate, or the feature they are written for?
:::

# China {.center}

Law first, then the firewall

## Law Built the Great Firewall

- **1996:** State Council *Interim Provisions* on international connection, **Art. 6**:
  international traffic must use **state-provided gateways**; no one may "establish or use
  other channels"
- **Jan 2017:** MIIT notice: no **cross-border channels (including VPNs)** without
  MIIT approval
- **Cybersecurity Law (2017), Art. 50:** authorities may order **technical measures to
  block** prohibited information from **outside China**
- **Art. 58:** with State Council approval, **temporary restrictions on network
  communications** in a region (a statutory basis for regional shutdowns)

The firewall is **infrastructure**, but its authority is **statute**.

::: {.notes}
• Callback to the GFW slides in the intro and protocols lectures: we studied *how* it filters; this is *why it is legal* to filter.<br>• Art. 6 is the chokepoint rule; Art. 14 of the same provisions is what is cited when someone is fined for "climbing the wall." Enforcement has mostly targeted VPN *sellers*, not users.<br>• Point to make: the 1996 rule predates the firewall; the law created the chokepoint before the technology used it.
:::

## The Cybersecurity Law Makes Every Operator a Censor

**Cybersecurity Law**: adopted **Nov 7, 2016**, in force **June 1, 2017**

- **Art. 12:** users may not use networks to incite **subversion** of the state, spread
  **separatism**, or **fabricate false information**
- **Art. 24:** operators must require **real identity** information, or refuse service
- **Art. 47:** on finding prohibited content, operators must **stop transmission, delete,
  keep records, and report**
- **Art. 37:** critical-infrastructure operators **store data in mainland China**

**Amended Oct 28, 2025; in force Jan 1, 2026:** higher fines, **extraterritorial** reach
to any overseas activity that harms China's cybersecurity, an explicit article on
**Party leadership**, and AI governance written into the statute.

::: {.notes}
• Compare Art. 47 to the DSA: in the EU the platform acts on notice; here it must *look* and act on its own. That is liability with a monitoring duty.<br>• Real-name: Freedom House says China has required it since at least 2012; Art. 24 put it in statute.<br>• Ask: if you were a foreign platform, which article would you fear most? (Usually 47.)<br>• The 2026 amendment did not change operator duties; it raised the stakes.
:::

## The Model Extends to AI and Identity

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Generative AI** (*Interim Measures*, in force **Aug 15, 2023**)

- **Art. 4(1):** "Uphold the **Core Socialist Values**"
- Must not generate content "inciting subversion," "harming the nation's image," or
  "fake and harmful information"
- Applies to **providers and users**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Cyberspace ID** (in force **July 15, 2025**)

- One state-issued **network ID** linked to a national ID and a **face scan**
- Formally **voluntary**; platforms may not ask for more ID from users who use it
- Critics: the state, not each platform, now holds the **identity map**
:::
:::

::: {.vignette}
**The pattern:** each new medium gets the **same content list**. The Art. 12 offences of
2017 reappear, nearly word for word, as rules for what a **chatbot may say** in 2023.
:::

::: {.notes}
• Callback to the AI-as-information-arbiter material: here the "alignment" target is written in law.<br>• Cyberspace ID: privacy framing from the state (platforms collect less); control framing from critics (one identity, held centrally). Let students argue both.<br>• Freedom House 2026 notes China now uses child-protection language to push further against anonymity.
:::

# Russia {.center}

From a sovereign network to a sovereign messenger

## The "Sovereign Internet" Law

**Federal Law 90-FZ** (May 1, 2019; in force **Nov 1, 2019**)

- Every ISP must install state-supplied **TSPU** boxes: DPI that can **filter, throttle,
  and reroute** traffic
- Creates a **national DNS** and powers to **centralize routing** in a "threat"
- Roskomnadzor operates the boxes; the **ISP no longer decides**

What it enabled (from our technical lectures):

- **Twitter throttled**, March 2021 (the `t.co` over-match)
- **YouTube degraded** from **July 2024**
- **ECH blocked** within a month of Cloudflare's rollout, **Nov 2024**

::: {.notes}
• This is the legal side of the TSPU case study in the throttling lecture. Ask a student to recall the `t.co` over-blocking.<br>• HRW 2019 called the provisions "overly broad and vague"; the law tells ISPs to install equipment without saying what it will be used for.<br>• Point to make: China built the chokepoint in 1996; Russia retrofitted one onto a commercial, decentralized Internet by statute.
:::

## Criminalizing Speakers and Readers

- **Mar 4, 2022** ("fakes" law, Criminal Code **Art. 207.3**): "knowingly **false
  information**" about the armed forces; up to **15 years** in prison
- **Dec 1, 2022** (foreign agents, **255-FZ**): anyone "**under foreign influence**" can
  be listed; no foreign money needs to be shown
- **Sept 1, 2025:** fines for **deliberately searching** for "**extremist**" material,
  including **over a VPN**, and for **advertising VPNs**
- **Dec 2025:** blocking of the most popular **VPN protocols** begins; **469 VPN services**
  blocked by Feb 2026

The target moved from **platforms** to **speakers** to **readers**.

::: {.notes}
• Walk the escalation: the 2022 laws punish what you say; the 2025 law punishes what you look for.<br>• "False" is defined by the Ministry of Defence's account; a journalist who reports a different casualty figure has spread a fake. Ask: how would a court decide what is "knowingly false" here?<br>• Foreign agents: the label must appear on everything the person publishes, a cost on speech without a ban.<br>• Callback to the circumvention lecture's VPN vignette.
:::

## Block the Foreign, Mandate the Domestic

::: {.vignette}
**Russia, 2025–26.**

- **June 2025:** law creates a **"national messenger"**: **Max**, built by VK. **Sept 1, 2025:**
  Max must be **preinstalled** on phones and tablets sold in Russia.
- **Aug 2025:** WhatsApp and Telegram **calls restricted**.
- **Feb 2026:** **YouTube, WhatsApp**, Facebook, and independent media **removed from the
  national DNS**; the Kremlin confirms the WhatsApp block (Feb 12).
- **Feb 2026:** a new law lets the **FSB order shutdowns without a court**, on grounds
  the president sets.
- **Apr 10, 2026:** OONI anomalies show **95%** of Telegram tests blocked; no formal ban
  was ever announced.
:::

Max is **not end-to-end encrypted**, and every Max account requires a **Russian or Belarusian
phone number**.

::: {.notes}
• This is the clearest case of law as both stick and carrot: block the foreign service, then legally require the domestic one.<br>• Note the method: the national DNS from the 2019 law was the instrument for the Feb 2026 blocks. Meduza found the DNS removal leaky at first (alternative resolvers still worked).<br>• Telegram: Meduza reports it has been unusable without a VPN for most users since mid-March, yet a Levada poll found 49% still read Telegram channels.<br>• Ask: is a preinstall mandate a censorship law? Compare app-store rules elsewhere.
:::

# Iran {.center}

Law delegates; the network executes

## Who Decides What Is Blocked

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Computer Crimes Law (2009)**

- **Art. 21–22:** a **Committee to Determine Instances of Criminal Content**, under the
  **Prosecutor General**, issues filtering orders
- **Art. 23:** hosts must comply **on receipt** of an order
- The **list of criminal content** is the committee's, not Parliament's
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Supreme Council of Cyberspace (2012)**

- Created by order of the **Supreme Leader**
- Sets filtering policy; drives the **National Information Network (NIN)**
- **Shutdowns** have no clear statutory basis: treated as **national-security** decisions
:::
:::

**Delegation is the design:** the law names a **body**, not a **rule**.

::: {.notes}
• Contrast with China and Russia, where offences are listed in statute (vaguely). Iran's law mostly delegates the list to a committee.<br>• Freedom House: shutdown decisions come from the Supreme National Security Council and are carried out by the ICT ministry through ISPs.<br>• Question for you: is "no law at all" worse or better than a vague law, for the person trying to contest a block?
:::

## From Protest Shutdowns to a Two-Tier Internet

- **Nov 2019:** fuel-price protests; the NIN keeps **banks, state apps, ride-hailing**
  running while the **global** Internet is cut
- **Sept 2022:** Mahsa Amini protests: **Instagram and WhatsApp** blocked (Sept 21),
  **mobile "curfews"** 4 pm–1 am
- **June 2025:** "stealth blackout" during the war, **BGP routes left up**

::: {.vignette}
**Freedom on the Net 2026** (Oct 2026): Iran fell from **13 to 9** out of 100.

- **Jan 2026:** near-total shutdown for **20 days** during the protests (from **Jan 8**)
- From **late Feb 2026:** about **88 days**, the **longest** nationwide shutdown FOTN has
  recorded
- By May 2026: **"Internet Pro"** plans sell global access at **~5×** the price, with
  consent to **surveillance**
:::

::: {.notes}
• The NIN is what makes long shutdowns affordable: domestic services keep running, so the state pays less for cutting the world off. Article 19 made this argument in 2020; 2026 is the proof.<br>• "Internet Pro" turns access into a licence: the price and the surveillance consent are the filter. Callback to the economic-controls segment later today.<br>• Date caution: Freedom House dates the long shutdown from late February; some outlets say March, and some count Jan 8 to May 26 as one blackout. Say "about 88 days, per Freedom House."<br>• Callback to the "Not Every Shutdown Withdraws the Route" slide in the protocols lecture.
:::

# The Template Travels {.center}

## Copying the Template: Vietnam and Turkey

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Vietnam, Decree 147** (in force **Dec 25, 2024**)

- Users must verify accounts with a **Vietnamese phone number** (or ID) before posting
- Platforms remove content within **24 hours** of an authority's request
- User data **stored locally**, handed over **on request**
- Only **verified** accounts may livestream
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Turkey, Law 5651** (2007, amended 2020 and 2022)

- Large foreign platforms must name a **local representative**
- Penalty ladder: ad ban, then **bandwidth cut 50%, then 90%**
- **2022:** Penal Code **Art. 217/A**, "publicly disseminating **misleading
  information**": 1–3 years
:::
:::

**Throttling as a legal sanction**: the penalty for a platform is written as a **bandwidth
percentage**.

::: {.notes}
• Vietnam: the parts are China's (real-name, 24-hour clock, localization), assembled by decree rather than statute.<br>• Turkey: a NATO member and EU candidate. The 90% throttle mostly worked as a threat; per Article 19, the major platforms set up local entities, and the penalty was not imposed for that reason.<br>• Callback: Turkey's 2014 DNS block of Twitter from the protocols lecture (the 8.8.8.8 graffiti).<br>• Ask: is a local-representative rule censorship? The DSA has a legal-representative rule too.
:::

## The Democratic Mirror: India

**IT Rules amendment** (notified **Feb 10, 2026**; in force **Feb 20, 2026**)

- Government takedown orders: act within **3 hours** (was **36**)
- **AI-generated** ("synthetically generated") content must carry **labels**
- Miss either and the platform risks its **safe harbour**

Context from earlier lectures: **65 shutdowns** in 2025, more than any other democracy.

**Question:** a 3-hour clock leaves no time to check an order. Is that different in kind
from Vietnam's 24 hours?

::: {.notes}
• This is the contrast case the comparison slide needs: an electoral democracy, with courts, using the same lever with a shorter clock than Vietnam's.<br>• Freedom House 2026 flags the 3-hour rule as pushing platforms toward removal; Amnesty warned of the same.<br>• Callback to the platform lecture's slide on state pressure running through platforms (India's earlier IT Rules amendments).<br>• Let the class argue before the next slide.
:::

# Same Lever, Different Law? {.center}

## Where Is the Line?

| | Democratic use | Authoritarian use | Question to argue |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Severity** | Fines, delisting | Prison (15 years), shutdowns, blocking | Does severity change the *kind* of law, or only its degree? |
| **Vagueness** | "Illegal content" defined elsewhere in law | "False," "extremist," "subversion" | Can any speech offence avoid vagueness? |
| **Recourse** | Courts, counter-notice, DSA appeal | Agency orders; courts not independent | Is recourse the real line? |
| **Transparency** | DSA database, Lumen | Secret lists, unpublished orders | Would publishing orders make these laws acceptable? |

**India, Turkey, the EU:** where on this table does each fall?

::: {.notes}
• This slide is for you to argue, not to read. Suggested questions to answer in your own words:<br>• (1) If recourse is the line, is the 3-hour Indian rule closer to Vietnam than to the DSA?<br>• (2) Germany's NetzDG had a 24-hour clock; was it authoritarian? Why not?<br>• (3) Do authoritarian laws borrow democratic language ("disinformation," "child safety," "sovereignty") on purpose? Russia cited fraud for the call blocks; China cites child protection for ID.<br>• (4) Which matters more for a platform's behaviour: the law's text or the court behind it?<br>• Say where you come down; that sentence becomes the thesis of §4.1.1.
:::

## Discussion

1. China and Russia both **block the foreign** and **mandate the domestic**. Is the
   mandate (Max, the NIN) the more powerful lever?
2. Iran now **sells** global access. Is "Internet Pro" a legal control, an economic one, or
   both?
3. Which democratic law from the last lecture would be **most dangerous** in the hands of
   a government that controls the courts?
4. Should a platform **comply, leave, or litigate**? WhatsApp left Russia by being
   blocked; others named local representatives in Turkey.

::: {.notes}
• Q2 is the bridge to the economic-controls segment.<br>• Q3 is the sharp one; push for a specific law (a takedown clock, a local-representative rule, age verification).<br>• Q4: tie to the countering lecture (Week 9), where exit is one lever.
:::

## Takeaways

- Authoritarian states use the **same legal levers** as democracies: licensing, liability,
  real names, localization, takedown clocks
- What changes the law is **vague offences**, **no independent recourse**, and **secrecy**
- The law **comes first**: China's 1996 gateway rule, Russia's 2019 TSPU mandate, Iran's
  filtering committee
- Newest step: **mandate the domestic** service and **price** the foreign one
- Democracies are **borrowing the clocks**; the line is recourse, not the lever
